catalog_quote: All of these correlates point to a general iambic pattern of stress. This is not to say, however, that Sorbung stress is predictable without reference to morphological structure. The following general principles seem to hold: 1. Minor syllables are never stressed. This may be due to the fact that the vowels in these syllables are epenthetic. 2. The last root syllable in a compound stem, not counting derivational suffixes, is stressed. 3. Two consecutive unstressed syllables are not tolerated. 4. Stress assignment is cyclic. ‘Underarm hair,’ from the compound cubˈlaa (cuup ‘breast’ plus laa ‘crotch’) plus míi ‘hair’ is cubˌlaaˈmíi rather than *ˌcuublaˈmíi. 5. Suffixes do not affect the stress of the base to which they are attached: ˈlook ‘big’, ˈloog-ˌoo ‘big-DECL’, ʔˈʉʉ ‘dog’, ʔˈʉʉ-e ‘dog-NOM’. 6. audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three quoted passages (deciding, domain, exception) found verbatim in the held JSEALS 4(1) PDF at the stated section and pages. Deciding source: a 2011 peer-reviewed phonological description from primary fieldwork, the only description of Sorbung in existence (Glottolog: 3 refs total, the other two being an 1837 one-page vocabulary and a 2014 PhD on a different, neighbouring lect). The classification 'morphological' (last root syllable of stem stressed, suffixes stress-neutral or lexically stressed/unstressed, cyclic, iambic/right-headed) is a faithful reading of the source's seven principles. No better or newer stress source exists; web checks (Glottolog languoid + reference records, Crossref) surfaced nothing further
